prompt: Read the following technical note and then answer the question at the end. A sparse mixture-of-experts language model has a shared dense path and many feed-forward experts. For each layer, a router chooses a small number of experts for every token. The selected experts have large quantized weight matrices. On a machine with limited GPU memory, the expert matrices can remain in RAM or file-backed mappings while dense tensors and the attention cache use GPU memory. Performance depends on both arithmetic and data movement. A decoding step normally handles one token, so the vector dot product is tuned for a single row. Prompt processing handles many tokens at once, so the same expert matrix is applied to several activation rows. In that multi-row case, repeatedly decoding the same quantized weights for every row can waste CPU work. A fused prefill kernel may decode each small weight block once, then reuse it for several activation rows. It must preserve the numerical semantics of the existing quantized vector-dot kernel. Correctness is established by comparing the output tensors against the reference implementation across multiple expert mappings and token counts. Performance is established separately by using the same model, prompt, context size, thread count, and runtime flags in both arms. The benchmark must report prompt processing time separately from generation time. A faster prefill path is useful even if single-token generation is unchanged, because long conversations, code files, and retrieved documents must first be processed into the context. However, a synthetic unit test alone is not enough: an end-to-end model request must produce the same deterministic response and show a repeatable reduction in prompt processing time. The experiment should remain isolated until both requirements are met. In this note, the CPU uses IQ2_S expert weights and Q8_K activations. The experimental path is enabled only for multiple activation rows; the existing vector-dot path stays active for a single row. This protects decode performance from unintended changes. The question is: what part of inference is this experiment designed to accelerate?
